Reuters contributed to this story.

articles.title: Dame Esther Rantzen: That's Life! presenter, Childline founder and assisted dying campaigner
articles.summary: The star presented That's Life! for two decades and set up two national helplines, including Childline.
articles.body:
Dame Esther Rantzen, who has died at the age of 86, was best known for presenting the BBC TV programme That's Life!

Over two decades, what started as a consumer programme with quirky asides became renowned for its high-profile campaigns, notably against child abuse.

It resulted in Dame Esther setting up Childline, a national telephone helpline for children suffering abuse or neglect.

She later became a renowned campaigner for older people and, in the last years of her life, for the legalisation of medically-assisted death.

Dame Esther Rantzen, broadcaster, campaigner and charity founder, dies aged 86

How That's Life! gave Esther Rantzen a career-defining moment

Esther Louise Rantzen was born in Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire on 22 June 1940. Her paternal ancestors were Polish Jews.

Her father, Henry, who worked as a broadcast engineer for the BBC, had moved the family out of London to escape German bombing during World War Two.

The family returned to London when the war ended. She later recalled she hated the grey streets of the capital after the semi-rural idyll in which she had spent her early childhood.

After a spell at a private school, run by what she recalled was a sadistic headmistress, she went to the North London Collegiate School in Edgware, and then to Somerville College, Oxford, where she read English.

She became an enthusiastic member of the Oxford University Dramatic Society and of the Experimental Theatre Group.

Rantzen then secured a job as a trainee studio manager with BBC Radio, before moving to television as a researcher on the satirical show BBC3, which had been created by Ned Sherrin.

She met documentary maker Desmond Wilcox when she approached him in a BBC bar and asked him to give a talk to a local youth club.

He asked her to dinner and offered her a job on Man Alive, the BBC's current affairs programme. The pair later began a relationship.

The relationship caused huge tensions in her department, not least because Wilcox's wife Patsy, one of Rantzen's best friends, also worked at the BBC.

By 1968, she was working on Braden's Week, a consumer programme fronted by Canadian presenter Bernard Braden.

A decision to allow the researchers a short spot on air gave Rantzen her first on-screen TV experience, where she made a favourable impression on the producers.

In 1972, Braden was sacked by the BBC after he appeared in a commercial for Stork margarine and his show was dropped.

A year later, the programme was resurrected, given a new title, That's Life! and Rantzen was selected as the main presenter.

Braden was sanguine about Rantzen's promotion but his wife, TV presenter Barbara Kelly, was publicly contemptuous of the decision and accused Wilcox of being instrumental in her appointment.

Launched in May 1973, That's Life! became an almost instant hit.

Recorded just before transmission on Saturday nights, it was initially a consumer protection programme investigating viewers' complaints about shoddy service and faulty goods.

Over the years it grew to include more quirky items.

It initiated the Jobsworth award for over-zealous bureaucrats and council officials, and Heap of the Week, in which failing domestic appliances would be destroyed on screen in a variety of ingenious ways.

Over the years, Rantzen was joined by a series of co-hosts, including Paul Heiney, Chris Searle and Bob Wellings, while the comedian Cyril Fletcher read his Odd Odes.

The show quickly became something of an institution but her relationship with Wilcox was causing problems behind the scenes.

Patsy Wilcox had reluctantly agreed to a divorce after Rantzen became pregnant, and Rantzen and Wilcox went on to marry in 1977.

But there were accusations from some BBC staff that Wilcox, who was her boss as well as her husband, was furthering her career, pointing out that BBC rules forbade married couples working together.

Wilcox resigned in 1980 and set up his own successful production company.

Rantzen also found time to devise a new talent series, The Big Time, which launched the career of singer Sheena Easton.

She became involved with the team behind the new ITV breakfast programme, TV-am, but dropped out before it went to air in 1983 so that she could remain at the BBC.

By the 1980s, That's Life! had expanded its remit away from basic consumer issues to take on the role of campaigner.

The appearance of Ben Hardwick, a child desperately in need of a liver transplant, launched a drive to raise the awareness of the need for organ donors. As a result, Ben received a new liver at the age of two, but died a year later.

Other campaigns helped introduce the replacement of hard surfaces in children's playgrounds with softer material and a change in the law to enforce the wearing of children's seat belts in the rear of cars.

Not everyone was happy with the new format and there were complaints that a serious, and sometimes emotionally draining sequence, was followed by a quirky item on, for example, rude-looking vegetables.

The programme continued to maintain its high viewing figures after a move to Sunday nights, but the television landscape was changing.

The BBC's show Watchdog and ITV's The Cook Report were bringing a much harder edge to consumer journalism.

The final That's Life! was broadcast on 19 June 1994 and featured a look back at both the highlights of the programme and Rantzen's own campaigning.

Possibly the most important and lasting result of any That's Life! campaign was the setting up of Childline in 1986. It followed a number of incidents, featured on the programme, including one in which a toddler had starved to death, locked in a bedroom.

Rantzen persuaded the BBC after the programme was transmitted that a helpline should be set up so that children suffering abuse or neglect could call in confidence. In the 48 hours it was open, it was inundated with calls.

This led to Rantzen campaigning for a 24/7 service to be set up. Childcare professionals claimed it would be impossible but she managed both to raise the money and persuade BT to provide premises and a free phone line.

By the time Childline merged with the NSPCC in 2006, it had 12 centres in the UK and the idea was quickly copied in many countries abroad.

Rantzen also devised and presented Hearts of Gold, a programme that celebrated previously unknown people who had been responsible for good deeds.

When That's Life! came off air, Rantzen continued to present her own afternoon talk show, entitled Esther, on BBC Two. It ran for 600 episodes and received two Bafta nominations.

Desmond Wilcox died in 2000 leaving Rantzen bereft. She wrote a series of articles about the problem of loneliness among older people, which she described as "a creeping enemy which erodes confidence."

She eventually set up The Silver Line, a 24/7 phone support system which offered advice, information and support to those who felt alone and unwanted.

Rantzen also went on to make an appearance on the ITV show I'm a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here in 2008.

She wrote a number of regular columns for newspapers and magazines and also involved herself with more than 50 charities.

Following the MPs' expenses scandal in 2009, Rantzen announced she would stand for parliament in Luton South.

She pitched herself against the sitting Labour MP, Margaret Moran, who had claimed expenses in excess of £23,000 for her second home in Southampton.

Moran stood down two days later but Rantzen fought the seat in the 2010 General Election, coming fourth with just over 4% of the vote.

Rantzen was made an OBE in 1991 and CBE in 2006. In the 2015 New Year Honours list, she was appointed a Dame Commander in recognition of the two helpline services she set up.

The following year she warned of the social media pressure on children in the digital world, urging families to "be aware" of the issue.

Speaking on Desert Island Discs in 2019, Dame Esther told presenter Lauren Laverne that her own broadcasting career would not be as successful if she had joined the industry now as a young woman, because she would not be "pretty enough".

In an interview with The Mirror in June 2023, she spoke about her diagnosis with stage-four lung cancer.

It "made me realise how very lucky I've been in my life," she said, "working with Childline and the Silver Line, and meeting so many fascinating and inspiring people".

"I'm not good at regrets. What I treasure most are the fantastic friendships I have made thanks to That's Life! during the last 50 years, the people I met, and the team who worked so hard, and laughed so hard, together for so long."

Six months later, she told The Times she did not expect to live much longer.

"Last January," she explained, "I assumed that I would probably not be around for my birthday in June, and that I'd definitely miss this Christmas.

"But when I met my oncologist I realised how ignorant I was and what gargantuan strides medicine has made recently.

"Has my diagnosis taught me any lessons valuable enough to pass on? The cliché is live each day as if it's your last and treasure every moment."

In December 2023, Dame Esther said that she was taking a "miracle" treatment for her lung cancer, adding that she might "buzz off to Zurich" - where assisted dying is legal - if it did not work.

A year later, she witnessed the House of Commons vote in favour of the first stage of a Bill that might make a medically-assisted death legal in England and Wales. A similar bill was introduced to the Scottish Parliament.

Although Dame Esther knew that she would not live long enough to take advantage of any new law, she said she wanted to protect other families from "the same agonising experience".

"In the olden days, doctors would ease you out of life and the difference was it wasn't necessarily with your consent," she said.

In March 2025, her daughter confirmed that the drug that had kept Dame Esther alive since her cancer diagnosis was no longer working. They had always known that its effects would be temporary.

Last December, she told a newspaper that she was planning "an 'official' Christmas with my children and five grandchildren, slightly ahead of the real Christmas so that there will be more chance that I am actually alive to enjoy it with them!"

In September 2026, the House of Commons voted against the Assisted Dying Bill, a decision Dame Esther described as "a tragic day".

She added that she was now too frail to travel to Switzerland to end her life.

"Everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now," she said, "which means that the people I love and care about either cannot visit me, or when they do, see me suffering pain or indignity which will inevitably get between them and our shared happy memories, and may even overwhelm the way they think of me."

The broadcaster and campaigner was once asked about what drove her to get involved in a multitude of causes.

"I need to be needed," she said. "It's what makes you get up in the morning, and makes you feel when you go to bed that the day has been well spent.

"There's a real pleasure in feeling somebody needs your help and that you actually have made a difference."

articles.title: Esther Rantzen: The story behind Nicholas Winton on That's Life!
articles.summary: Sir Nicholas Winton's story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988.
articles.body:
Dame Esther Rantzen's commitment to charitable causes is something she will forever be remembered for.

Along with founding Childline, a helpline for children, and The Silver Line, which supports older people struggling with loneliness, she also created a broadcasting legacy during her time on That's Life!

She presented the hugely popular BBC One show from 1973 to 1994, helping transform it from a consumer rights programme to an issues-based series, drawing in huge audiences.

One of her most memorable career moments came during one particular episode in 1988 - the footage of which has gone viral several times over in recent years.

Dame Esther had been told the story of Nicholas Winton, the man who had organised the rescue of 669 children from Czechoslovakia, which was occupied in 1939 by Nazi forces.

Sir Nicholas was able to rescue the mainly Jewish cohort of children after briefly visiting Prague.

He was knighted in 2003 for his humanitarian work.

Sir Nicholas, who was born to German-Jewish parents, made a list of the children that needed sponsorship and found homes for them to go to in Britain.

He worked alongside activists and humanitarians in Czechoslovakia to navigate complex political obstacles, such as getting children to Britain through the Netherlands, which had closed its borders to Jewish refugees.

Sir Nicholas was ultimately successful due to a House of Commons ruling on allowing young refugees in the country, which had been passed a couple of months before his rescue mission began.

With the help of his mother, he put photos of the children in British magazines such as Picture Post to help find them homes and organised for hostels to take in some refugees too.

He managed to raise money to cover travel for the children and provide them with essentials when they reached British soil.

His incredible work went largely unreported for nearly 50 years - until his wife found a scrapbook in their loft, which contained names of children he had rescued.

It was given to Holocaust researchers, who helped track down some of the children he had helped.

Sir Nicholas' story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988 and Dame Esther Rantzen told viewers about his story.

Speaking in February 2024, Dame Esther said when she first got in touch with Sir Nicholas, who she called Nicky, she "congratulated him on his extraordinary achievement".

She told The Radio Times he had expressed some disappointment about his efforts, commenting that "not enough" people had been saved.

"I was devastated that he felt he had failed. I wanted to prove to this extraordinary man that every life he had saved was precious," Dame Esther added.

She invited him onto That's Life and during his first appearance, his scrapbook was shared with the audience, and two women he had saved as children - Vera Gissing and Lady Milena Grenfell-Baines - revealed their identities to him on TV.

They were sitting either side of Sir Nicholas, who had no idea of the surprise - something Dame Esther recalled as "incredibly moving".

Lady Milena is one of the most well-recognised Holocaust survivors in the UK.

She left Prague with her younger sister Eva at the age of nine, travelling on a special train arranged by Winton.

The two sisters were looked after by a Tameside family until their mother arrived the following year, having escaped via Norway.

Gissing, who was rescued from Prague in 1939 at the age of 11, lost most of her family during the Holocaust and ended up settling in the UK after the war ended.

"That was the only time in my career when I had to stop recording to wipe away my tears," Dame Esther also said.

The production team at That's Life were then contacted by several viewers who had watched the show and realised their connection to Sir Nicholas.

That gave the show's team an idea which would go on to become one of British television's most famous moments.

"In our next episode, I asked all those who owed their lives to him to stand, and Nicky, whom we had seated on the front row, turned to see the whole ground floor of the Television Theatre on their feet," Dame Esther recalled.

1988: Holocaust hero Nicholas Winton on That's Life

This is a TV moment many will remember and in subsequent years has been rediscovered by new audiences thanks to social media.

Dame Esther said she watched the episode "many times" and "each time found myself deeply moved".

She says she kept in contact with Sir Nicholas, meeting regularly until his death in 2015 at the age of 106.

They would always have a connection due to the TV show, but Dame Esther said hearing the stories of the children he had saved also made her feel "immensely lucky" to have been a Jew born in England in the 1940s.

Sir Nicholas' work has been the subject of a number of different films and documentaries, most recently the biopic One Life.

Starring Sir Anthony Hopkins , the film premiered at the Toronto Film Festival and was released in the UK in January 2024.

Dame Esther said it had been estimated "that 6, 000 people owe their very existence to Nicholas Winton".

She added: "The Jewish children Nicky rescued were almost the only ones in Czechoslovakia to survive the Holocaust".

And thanks to Dame Esther relaying his story to viewers on That's Life!, millions of people are now aware of the huge impact Sir Nicholas had.

Dame Esther Rantzen, broadcaster, campaigner and charity founder, dies aged 86

articles.title: MIKE DAVIS: The American gun-free zone you didn't know about
articles.summary: The High Court of American Samoa ruled the Second Amendment doesn't apply in the unincorporated territory, allowing a near-total gun ban to take effect.
articles.body: In October 2024, the High Court of American Samoa, an unincorporated territory of the United States, issued a staggering ruling that received little media attention. The justices ruled that, since American Samoa is unincorporated, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms does not apply there. The ruling allowed a near-total gun ban to take effect. President Donald Trump and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum can and must reverse this immediately. The issue of territories is obscure, so some background is helpful. The United States has 50 states and several territories, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa. The District of Columbia also is not a state; however, unlike the other territories, it receives three electoral votes for the presidency pursuant to the 23rd Amendment. None of these territories receives voting representation in Congress, though delegates from the territories can sit on congressional committees and, for instance, serve as managers for the House during a Senate impeachment trial. These territories generally have courts, such as the U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico and the U.S. District Court for the District of the Virgin Islands. Presidents nominate judges to these courts, and the Senate confirms them. As Article IV judges, those on these courts serve with a tenure of 10 years, and litigants may appeal their rulings through the relevant circuits. When territories violate constitutional rights, individual litigants or the Justice Department can sue them in federal court. President Trump's Justice Department did precisely that last year, accusing the U.S. Virgin Islands of enacting gun restrictions that run afoul of the Second Amendment. LAWYER WHO BEAT HAWAII GUN LAW CALLS STATE’S RELIANCE ON BLACK CODE ‘DISGRACEFUL’ American Samoa differs judicially and in other ways from the other territories. No statute grants birthright citizenship to those born in American Samoa, unlike every other territory. American Samoa also has no federal court, unlike other territories. The High Court of American Samoa serves as the ultimate judicial authority in that territory. 48 U.S.C. § 1661 vests the president with civil, military and judicial control over American Samoa. A 1951 executive order by President Harry Truman delegated authority over the territory to the secretary of the interior. Article III, Section 3 of American Samoa's territorial constitution grants the secretary of the interior the power to appoint justices to the High Court. These justices serve no life tenure, unlike federal judges who serve during good behavior. The secretary can remove American Samoa justices without cause and appoint replacements without Senate confirmation. President Trump and Secretary Burgum must act in light of the court's ruling against the Second Amendment. That amendment stands as a cornerstone of the Republic, and the Supreme Court reaffirmed its vitality recently in Wolford v. Lopez. Hawaii decided that it did not wish to comply with the Supreme Court's recent Second Amendment precedents. It implemented an absurdly restrictive concealed-carry regime under which gun owners could bring their weapons onto properties only where signs expressly permitted them. The Hawaii Supreme Court relied on, among other ridiculous rationales, the so-called "Aloha Spirit" to justify this infringement. Hawaii argued that, prior to statehood, no right to gun ownership existed. The Supreme Court, over a dissent from its three liberal justices, rejected that rationale. The Second Amendment applies just as much in Hawaii as it does in Chicago, New York and the District of Columbia. DOJ TARGETS SPANBERGER, NEWSOM GUN LAWS WITH TWIN LAWSUITS AFTER SCOTUS AFFIRMS SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS No lawsuit is even necessary in American Samoa. The broad authority Congress granted the president under Section 1661 empowers President Trump and Secretary Burgum to overrule this egregious decision. Federal courts have upheld this overruling authority in several cases, though the Supreme Court has never addressed the question squarely. Beyond firing the justices and appointing new ones who respect the Constitution, President Trump should make clear in an executive order that the Second Amendment applies with equal force in American Samoa as it does in states and other territories. The First Amendment is foundational to the Republic. The Second Amendment is no different, no matter how hard anti-gun zealots work to obscure that truth. The current justices of the High Court of American Samoa have stripped it of any force whatsoever. The administration holds a simple, swift and lawful remedy, and they must use it. articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: State Department revokes over 250,000 visas in broad immigration vetting crackdown
articles.summary: The State Department has revoked over 250,000 visas under Trump for criminal activity, fraud, birth tourism and national security threats.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: The State Department has revoked more than 250,000 visas since President Donald Trump took office, as the administration continues to crack down on unlawful immigration and increase vetting of who is allowed to visit the United States. The revocations were for a variety of violations, including visa holders who violated the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against the U.S. or Americans, defrauded Americans, abused the immigration system, and endangered national security, a State Department official told Fox News Digital. Among the visas revoked were 2,300 in connection with birth tourism, the practice of pregnant foreign nationals traveling to the U.S. specifically to give birth so their child automatically receives citizenship. BIRTH TOURISM SCAMS DRAW SWEEPING CRACKDOWN AS VISA REVOCATIONS CLIMB "Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, the State Department has now revoked more than 250,000 visas — a historic milestone that reflects our unwavering commitment to protecting the American people," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said. "Every visa decision is a national security decision. Through continuous vetting on a scale never seen before, we are identifying and removing those who commit crimes, support terrorism, defraud Americans, or abuse our immigration system," Pigott added. "A U.S. visa is a privilege, not a right — and if you violate the terms of that privilege, you will lose it. We will not stop until every foreign national who threatens the safety of our communities is held accountable." On Monday, the State Department revoked the visas of 27 Latin American officials, former officials, and their families over accusations of corruption. The officials are from Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. Over the summer, the Trump administration began preparing to revoke business and tourist visas held by as many as 200,000 foreigners who have applied for asylum in the U.S. DHS' TOP LAWYER THREATENS PENALTIES FOR ATTORNEYS CLOGGING ASYLUM SYSTEM The effort would target B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to foreigners who later sought asylum. At the time, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau said Americans were "fed up" with "bogus asylum claims." "Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration laws; rather, it’s supposed to provide a narrow safe harbor for persons persecuted because of their ‘race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion,’" he wrote on X at the time. TRUMP ADMIN PAUSES VISA APPOINTMENTS WORLDWIDE AMID HEIGHTENED SCREENING FOR APPLICANTS He noted that frivolous claims have swamped the system, which could take years to adjudicate whether applicants are entitled to asylum in the U.S. In August, the State Department also revoked more than 175,000 visas. The majority of those were revoked due to law enforcement encounters for a range of criminal activity, with assault, driving under the influence, theft and drug crimes being the leading causes. articles.title: Dame Esther Rantzen: That's Life! broadcaster and charity campaigner dies at 86
articles.summary: Dame Esther presented the BBC show That's Life! for 21 years and launched the charity Childline.
articles.body:
Dame Esther Rantzen, who presented BBC show That's Life! for 21 years and launched the Childline charity, has died at the age of 86.

The broadcaster hosted and produced That's Life! during its run from 1973 to 1994. It regularly attracted 20 million viewers for its mixture of serious consumer investigations and light-hearted items.

Dame Esther launched Childline, a British counselling service for children and young people, in 1986, and in 2013 she launched Silver Line to help elderly people suffering from isolation and loneliness.

She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In December 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic.

But in a statement given to the Press Association in September 2026, she said that despite having "spent the money and made the plans" to go to Dignitas, she had since reached the point where she was "too physically fragile to make the journey".

The prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying added that the law must "change and change quickly", as she renewed her plea ahead of the latest debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill.

The broadcaster revealed her cancer diagnosis in January 2023, saying the news had prompted her to express "profound thanks to everyone who has made my life so joyful".

Rantzen joined BBC radio as a sound effects assistant before becoming a TV researcher, and in 1968 she trained as a producer and director.

The young broadcaster became a researcher and reporter for Bernard Braden's consumer affairs programme, Braden's Week.

When That's Life! launched in 1973, she was its figurehead and became a popular fixture on screens as the show's formidable and fun-loving presenter and producer.

The consumer show's notable items, according to her website , included "talking dogs, Jobsworth Awards and campaigns on behalf of abused children, organ transplants, safe playgrounds, and to provide justice for consumers".

Its most-viewed episode featured Sir Nicholas Winton being introduced for the first time to survivors he had saved from the Holocaust, during a 1988 instalment of the show.

Later in her career, she also appeared on Strictly Come Dancing, First Dates and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here!

Dame Esther was married to documentary film-maker Desmond Wilcox from 1977 until he died in 2000. They had three children.

She was made a dame in 2015 for her services to children and older people.

In December 2024, Dame Esther spoke of her "great relief" after MPs backed proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales.

In an interview with the Sunday Times in late November 2025, she said her "great hope for 2026" was the potential passing of the assisted dying bill , saying "as long as others in the future will be able to ask for help to die as they choose, I will die happy".

The latest debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill took place on 11 September, when MPs voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270 - a majority of 16 - against the proposed legislation.

Disability campaigners described the result as a "victory". Dame Esther told the BBC of her "disappointment" with the outcome, saying: "I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it's a tragic day."

articles.title: 24,057 Vijayawada families get ownership rights to decades-old house sites
articles.summary: 24,057 Vijayawada families get ownership rights as CM Naidu distributes regularisation pattas across 617 acres in eight constituencies under Pedalaku Pattabhishekam.
articles.body: Vijayawada: Thousands of families in Vijayawada who have lived for decades on house sites without full ownership rights received major relief on Wednesday, with chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu handing over regularisation pattas under the ‘Pedalaku Pattabhishekam’ programme at Makineni Basavapunnaiah Stadium in Singh Nagar.The regularisation gives 24,057 families full ownership rights over house sites covered by pattas issued decades ago during the NTR regime. The exercise covers 617 acres, or 29.86 lakh square yards, across 15 mandals and eight assembly constituencies in NTR and Krishna districts. The govt has estimated the land being regularised at Rs 9,800 crore, while its market value is around Rs 24,297 crore.The issue had remained unresolved for decades, particularly for families living in houses built on hill areas in Vijayawada East, West and Central constituencies. Residents had been seeking legal recognition of their properties, with the absence of complete ownership rights leaving them without secure title over homes they had occupied for years.The beneficiaries are spread across Vijayawada East, Vijayawada West, Vijayawada Central, Gannavaram, Jaggayyapeta, Mylavaram, Nandigama and Tiruvuru constituencies. Vijayawada East has the highest number of beneficiaries at 7,990, followed by Vijayawada West with 7,465 and Vijayawada Central with 5,815.According to the govt data released ahead of the programme, the beneficiaries include 12,093 BC families, 6,130 OC families, 4,546 SC families, 955 Muslim BC families and 333 ST families.Addressing the gathering, Naidu said the govt had resolved a long-pending problem faced by families who had been living on the sites for decades. He said the ownership rights would provide legal security to the beneficiaries and urged them to safeguard the properties for their future generations.Naidu said the Vijayawada exercise was part of a wider effort to resolve old house-site ownership issues in the state. A similar exercise in Visakhapatnam had earlier provided full ownership rights to 28,445 families over residential land valued by the govt at Rs 8,874 crore.The chief minister also said the govt was working to resolve other long-pending land and property issues and described the distribution of pattas as an effort to provide property security to poor families.The programme was attended by ministers Nadendla Manohar, Anagani Satya Prasad and Satya Kumar Yadav, besides MPs, MLAs and other public representatives from NTR and Krishna districts.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Vijayawada | Silver Rate in Vijayawada | Bank Holidays in Vijayawada | Public Holidays in Vijayawada | Petrol Price in Vijayawada | Diesel Price in Vijayawada | CNG Price in Vijayawada | LPG Price in VijayawadaStay updated with the latest Vijayawada news. articles.summary: Dhamnod police arrested Rohit Gangare, wanted in a human trafficking case with a Rs 3,000 reward, accused of luring a woman, selling her, and assaulting her.
articles.body: Mhow: Dhamnod police on Wednesday arrested Rohit Gangare (29), a long-absconding suspect in a human trafficking racket who carried a cash reward of Rs 3,000.Gangare, a resident of Sala rehabilitation area under Dhamnod police jurisdiction, was arrested following technical analysis and information from an informant.Dhamnod police registered a case against Gangare after a woman accused him of trafficking, confinement and assault, station in-charge Santosh Yadav said.The woman reported on Dec 10, 2021, that Gangare had enticed her with a marriage proposal and an offer of Rs 50,000 before taking her to Guntur, Andhra Pradesh. articles.title: State-of-the-art urban and inter-city passenger bus services begin in city
articles.summary: AICTSL launches new urban, inter-city buses in Indore under Mukhyamantri Sugam Parivahan and PM e-Bus Sewa; 70 e-buses, GPS, CCTV, UPI ticketing.
articles.body: Indore: Atal Indore City Transport Services Limited launched new state-of-the-art urban and inter-city passenger bus services on Wednesday under Mukhyamantri Sugam Parivahan Seva and PM e-Bus Sewa schemes.Water resources minister Tulsiram Silawat, MP Shankar Lalwani, MLAs Madhu Verma, Mahendra Hardia and Malini Gaud, and district collector Shivam Verma flagged off the new fleet at the AICTSL complex. The dignitaries and passengers then joined the inaugural trip.Speaking at the event, Silawat called the revival of organised public transport services after two decades a major milestone for regional connectivity.Under Mukhyamantri Sugam Parivahan Seva, AICTSL will operate buses from Indore to intra-state and inter-state destinations, including Dhar, Ujjain, Bhopal, Jabalpur, Rewa, Ratlam, Khandwa, Omkareshwar, Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Udaipur and Nagpur.Under the PM e-Bus Sewa initiative, 70 electric air-conditioned buses are operational, with plans to expand the fleet to 150. The transit network includes dedicated bus stops, charging stations and a centralised monitoring system linking key cities, metropolitan areas and pilgrimage sites.All buses are equipped with panic buttons for women’s safety, CCTV surveillance, live GPS tracking, digital and UPI ticketing, and concession passes for students and persons with disabilities to improve passenger safety and operational efficiency.AICTSL executive director Arth Jain said, “The initiative aims to establish a safe, sustainable, and citizen-centric public transport network across Western Madhya Pradesh.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Indore | Silver Rate in Indore | Bank Holidays in Indore | Public Holidays in Indore | Petrol Price in Indore | Diesel Price in Indore | CNG Price in Indore | LPG Price in IndoreStay updated with the latest Indore news. articles.title: Transnational repression from China far-reaching: US Congressman after meeting Dalai Lama
articles.summary: US Rep. Brian Mast warns China’s transnational repression is far-reaching after meeting the Dalai Lama, backing Tibetans’ right to choose the next Dalai Lama.
articles.body: Dharamshala: Days after Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States, a bipartisan delegation from the US Congress, led by Brian Mast, chairperson of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, met the Dalai Lama at his residence in Dharamshala on Wednesday and reaffirmed support for the Tibetan people and the preservation of their cultural and religious identity. In a strongly worded message, the delegation said that China cannot manufacture the next Dalai Lama and that the Tibetans must be free to determine their own religious future.The delegation included Brian Mast, James Gallagher, Jimmy Patronis, Haley Stevens and Shrinivas Prasad Thanedar. Congressman Brian Mast delivered a stark warning about Beijing’s plans for the Dalai Lama’s reincarnation, saying, “If that means abducting somebody, they will do it. If that means abducting a whole family, they will do it. If that means naming their own lama, they will do it.” Mast pointed to China’s alleged past abductions of individuals connected to the succession process, saying they were “never seen again.” Mast said the threat of transnational repression from China was far-reaching, alleging that Beijing could extend such activities to any other country.Mast said that China and the freedom of the Tibetan people were among the top issues discussed during the meeting. “Certainly, China was among the top issues, the freedom of the people of Tibet, his representation of freedom across the globe, just as we believe that the United States is a representation of freedom across the globe. We discussed a great many things,” Mast said. He also said the Dalai Lama believes the US President meeting with the Chinese President would not affect concerns over the treatment of Tibetans. “His Holiness believed that it was important that President Trump meet with Xi Jinping. They are two leaders of the world’s biggest and strongest countries across the globe. So yes, it’s very important, and it should happen,” Mast said.“It doesn’t take away in any way from believing that China should not be repressing its people, should not be repressing the Tibetan people or the Uyghur people, but rather working to embrace freedom and support freedom across the globe,” he said.Congresswoman Haley Stevens said the delegation wanted to highlight the plight of the Tibetan people and support their freedom. “I joined chairman Brian Mast in this historic and important visit for the plight of the Tibetan people as it exists here in Dharamshala and as we want to see Tibet remain free,” Stevens said. articles.summary: Hisar court sentences Vikas to 20 years rigorous imprisonment and Rs 71,000 fine for drugging and raping a 13-year-old student after luring her.
articles.body: Hisar: A court here has sentenced a man to 20 years of rigorous imprisonment for luring away a 13-year-old Class X student and raping her after allegedly drugging her. Additional District and Sessions Judge Sunil Jindal also imposed a fine of Rs 71,000 on the convict, Vikas. The case was registered on Nov 30, 2021, following the incident on Nov 29.According to police, the victim came in contact with Vikas while travelling to and from her tuition classes. On Nov 29, around 4.30pm, he allegedly lured her on the pretext of going for a stroll and took her to Hisar bus stand. He then allegedly took her to Jindal Park and gave her a burger. After eating it, the girl lost consciousness. When she regained consciousness, she realised something was wrong.The accused allegedly threatened to kill her if she told anyone. He then reportedly attempted to take her to Delhi by train and molested her along the way before bringing her back to Hisar and abandoning her at Barwala bus stand.The girl later narrated the ordeal to her mother. articles.title: Covington County Sheriff’s Department seeking tips in August 20, 2025 disappearance of Brandi White
articles.summary: The search continues for Brandi White, who was last seen in August 2025 near Highway 532 and William Warren Road in the Mount Olive, Mississippi, area. The Covington County Sheriff’s Department is investigating.
articles.body: Brandi Lauren White’s aunt describes her niece as resilient. “She’s been through hell and back through her whole life,” Angela Cordell told Dateline. At around 20 years old, Brandi was beaten and raped, and spent three months in a coma, according to her aunt. “She came out of that, you know, and had to learn how to walk again and talk again and everything,” Angela said. “But she survived it.” Angela told Dateline that Brandi was able to find joy again after that experience. She said you could always hear Brandi’s laughter over anyone else’s in a room. Brandi eventually became a mother. She has a teen son and a young daughter. “She loved her babies,” Angela said. “She was a people person,” Angela said. But Angela said her trusting nature could also be her downfall. “‘Cause she trusted the wrong people, you know?” Angela says her niece struggled with drug addiction and cycled in and out of rehab. In the summer of 2025, it seemed like something had shifted. Brandi had completed another stay in treatment and was determined to rebuild. “When she first got out of rehab, you know, she was like, ‘OK, I’m gonna try to make it,’” Angela recalled. Brandi went back to her old job at a gas station, and she seemed to be on a better path until she began spending time with people from her past, according to Angela. And then, she vanished. More than a year later, Brandi’s family is still waiting for answers. Chief Deputy Ricky Lott of the Covington County Sheriff’s Department told Dateline Brandi was last seen around 3 a.m. on August 20, 2025, near Highway 532 and William Warren Road in the Mount Olive, Mississippi, area. Lott says it is a wooded area that had been cleared and was being used as a dumpsite. The site was a former gravel pit where people had long hauled away dirt, then filled the holes in with trash. “As the trash piles up, they, you know, they bury it,” he said. According to Lott, 37-year-old Brandi had been staying with a family friend for about 10 days and was with that person when she was last seen. Angela, who is acting as the family spokesperson, says the friend told Brandi’s father that he and Brandi ran off in different directions, after apparently getting spooked by something. “I don’t know if they thought it was the police or whatever.” But when the family friend came back, Brandi was gone. “He ran back to his car and was hollering for Brandi.” But the family friend could not find her. The Covington County Sheriff’s Office arrived on the scene, where a group was already looking for Brandi. During the search, investigators recovered a shoe, which is being held as evidence. “Nobody was able to confirm that it was her shoe,” Lott said. The dump site has since closed. Before her disappearance, Lott said, the longest Brandi had ever gone without contacting her family was a couple of weeks. That lengthy silence has prompted investigators to consider the unimaginable. “What we do here would be to look for a body,” he said. “Or look for, you know, if she was, you know, killed and disposed of someplace.” Investigators have also considered the possibility that drug use played a role. “There’s a possibility she could have overdosed and whoever she was with may have panicked and didn’t know what to do,” he said. However, he emphasized that these theories remain speculative. Lott says investigators have conducted numerous interviews but found no evidence of foul play. And the family friend “still remains a suspect at this time,” he said. “We haven’t been able to clear him completely.” Dateline reached out to the family friend but has not yet heard back. The Covington County Sheriff’s Department continues to look into the tips being submitted, “but it is just pure speculation,” Lott said. What they need is someone who knows what happened to come forward and “help us out,” he stressed. “We want to get closure for the family. We want to solve this case, and -- and if it was an accident, then we’ll investigate it that way,” Lott said. “If it was something intentional, then we need to investigate it that way also.” More than a year later, Brandi’s family just wants her to come home. “Brandi is loved by everybody in her family. Everybody loves her,” her aunt Angela said. Brandi’s children are staying with her father, according to Angela. They miss their mother. “She would do anything to make sure they had what they needed,” Angela said. Before she disappeared, Brandi taught her son how to drive. “He loves her, and he’s hoping for her to come home.” Brandi is 5’3’’, 130 lbs. She has brown and blond hair and blue eyes. She would be 38 years old today. If you have any information about Brandi’s disappearance, please contact the Covington County Sheriff’s Department at 601-765-8281.
